The key distinction is that **“legal to compete in” is not the same as “licensed as a sport nationwide.”** The U.S. has no single national regulator for most combat sports. State and tribal rules govern events, and the definition of a regulated contest varies: a discipline may require commission approval in one place, be overseen by a commission-approved sanctioning organization elsewhere, or fall outside that jurisdiction’s rules. There isn’t a reliable single list of every sport that is licensable in every state. For a specific event, check the law and commission rules where it will take place. <citation src="23,24"></citation>

### How the system is organized

- **Regulators:** State athletic, boxing, or combative-sports commissions—and, for events on tribal lands, potentially tribal commissions—set and enforce local requirements. Depending on the jurisdiction, they may license fighters, promoters, officials, and event personnel; approve events; and impose medical and safety rules. The Association of Boxing Commissions and Combative Sports (ABC) is a coordinating association of regulators, **not a federal regulator**. <citation src="3,14,23"></citation>
- **Sanctioning organizations:** These are separate from government regulators. Where a state delegates oversight—especially for amateur events—the commission may authorize particular organizations to supervise events. New York, for example, provides for licensed “Authorized Sanctioning Entities” across specified sports. An organization’s rules or national presence do not by themselves make it an authorized sanctioner in every state. <citation src="24"></citation>
- **Promotions, leagues, and federations:** A promotion such as UFC puts on events; a national or international federation organizes participation and competition under its rules; a commission regulates events within its jurisdiction. Those roles overlap sometimes, but they are not interchangeable.

### Main categories and where to look

| Sport or event type | Typical oversight and organizations to investigate | Strong starting points for records |
|---|---|---|
| **Professional boxing** | State or tribal commission; ABC coordinates among commissions. The Muhammad Ali Boxing Reform Act concerns professional boxing. The sport has promoters and independent title sanctioning bodies, but neither replaces the event regulator. | The relevant commission’s event results and records; BoxRec and Fight Fax are commonly used record sources, but check the commission for official jurisdictional records. The ABC site also has an Event & Bout Data area. <citation src="13,14"></citation> |
| **Amateur/Olympic-style boxing** | State/local event rules still matter. USA Boxing is the U.S. national governing organization for its amateur and Olympic pathway; it is not the regulator for every professional boxing card. | USA Boxing event pages, athlete information, rules, and competition results; a public API was not established by the sources reviewed. <citation src="6,7"></citation> |
| **Professional and amateur MMA** | State or tribal commission, sometimes with a commission-approved sanctioner for amateur events. UFC, PFL, and other promoters run promotions; they do not regulate the whole sport. ABC publishes unified rules and regulatory resources. | Commission event results and suspension records; the ABC identifies shared record-keeping resources for MMA. <citation src="13,14,23"></citation> |
| **Kickboxing and Muay Thai** | Frequently regulated with boxing and MMA, but rules and delegation differ by state. USA Muaythai is the U.S. national federation associated with IFMA and recognized by the USOPC; professional and amateur event approval remains jurisdiction-dependent. | State commission or authorized sanctioner for event records; USA Muaythai for federation competitions and national-team information. <citation src="22,23,24"></citation> |
| **Grappling, Brazilian jiu-jitsu, judo, karate, taekwondo, and wrestling** | Treatment depends especially on whether the event involves striking, whether it is professional or amateur, and the state’s statutory definitions. Some states expressly include grappling or non-professional wrestling; others’ rules focus on blows. New York lists several of these among sports for which sanctioning entities may be licensed. | The state commission or sanctioner for regulated events; national governing bodies and event organizers for their own competitions. <citation src="23,24"></citation> |
| **Professional wrestling entertainment** | Often a distinct category from competitive amateur wrestling, and its regulatory treatment varies by state. Don’t assume that an event is exempt—or commission-regulated—without checking local law. | State agency for licensing or event rules; the promotion and specialist databases for match histories and results. |

This is a **map of the major categories, not a 50-state legal determination**. “Wrestling,” for example, can mean collegiate or Olympic-style competition, submission grappling, or scripted professional entertainment, which may be treated very differently. Some jurisdictions also regulate other forms of unarmed combat. <citation src="23,24"></citation>

### Data and API picture

For research, start with the **authority closest to the data**: the event’s commission for jurisdictional results, a federation for its own tournaments, and a promotion for its card and athlete material. A public webpage is not necessarily an official record, and an official website does not necessarily offer a public API.

- **Government commissions and the ABC:** These are high-value sources for event outcomes, licensing, and suspensions. The ABC site exposes regulatory materials and event/bout data, but the sources reviewed do **not** establish a public, documented API for commission bout records. Treat it as a web/database source unless the ABC or a commission confirms an API or data-access arrangement. <citation src="13"></citation>
- **BoxRec / Fight Fax / MMARegistry:** These are record-keeping or record-reference resources, not regulators. The ABC-related material identifies BoxRec for professional boxing and MMARegistry for MMA records; access arrangements and machine-readable availability should be checked directly. <citation src="14"></citation>
- **Federations:** USA Boxing and USA Muaythai provide public competition, athlete, rules, or event information. I found no evidence in the reviewed sources of a documented, open public API from either. <citation src="6,7,22"></citation>
- **Commercial or third-party APIs:** Sportradar documents a paid MMA API with schedules, results, competitor profiles, rankings, and statistics, but its stated event coverage is UFC-focused—not a national feed of all U.S.-sanctioned combat sports. A third-party boxing API advertises U.S. commission-sanctioned results with coverage currently described as Nevada-first; verify its coverage, provenance, and data rights before relying on it. <citation src="18,8"></citation>
- **Unofficial or hobby APIs:** Community-built UFC APIs exist, but they are not UFC or commission authorities; one reviewed project explicitly limits its data to personal, non-commercial use. Don’t treat an API’s existence as permission to reuse the underlying data commercially. <citation src="16"></citation>

**Practical research workflow:** choose the discipline, professional/amateur status, and event location; identify the relevant commission; check its statute, rules, and approved sanctioners; then collect results from the commission or the applicable federation. For each source, record coverage dates, event jurisdiction, whether results are final or provisional, and licensing/API terms. This avoids mistaking a league’s data for a complete or authoritative national record.
